podcast.body: Despite not being a chart hit in its original release year (1977), "Heroes" has been commercially redeemed in the digital age, becoming one of Bowie's most beloved songs. The week he died, it was his fifth most played catalog song on Spotify, and it re-entered the Rock and Alternative Songs chart in January 2026 after its use in Netflix's "Stranger Things." "And one Bowie favorite that has been commercially redeemed in the digital age is 1977's Heroes."

podcast.body: The title track from David Bowie's 1977 album, recorded in Berlin, features notable contributions from King Crimson guitarist Robert Fripp. Fripp's part involved creating three distinct feedback loops from his guitar (an A note four feet from the amp, a G note three feet from the amp, and a similar third take) which were then processed through an EMS synthesizer. The song also incorporates piano, early synthesizers, a special microphone setup, and a Chamberlain keyboard, creating a rich texture with significant distortion and feedback. "Bowie with Robert Fripp contributing some distortion and feedback."

podcast.body: The title track of Bowie's 1977 album, "Heroes" is now one of his most cherished songs and considered a masterpiece, though it was underrated at the time (peaking at #24 in the UK, missing the US Hot 100). Its lyrics depict two lovers by the Berlin Wall during the Cold War. The recording features Brian Eno's oscillating electronic pulse, Robert Fripp's guitar drone, and Tony Visconti's innovative gated microphone system for Bowie's vocal, making it thunderous and anthemic. "Majestic, histrionic, soaring, ruminative, enigmatic, yet regal. Heroes has been called David Boey's masterpiece."

podcast.body: The titular single from the *Heroes* album, despite its current iconic status, initially went largely unnoticed upon its release. Its widespread popularity wasn't achieved until David Bowie's performance at Live Aid in 1985. "el single Heroes pasó bastante de saber si evidó su momento. No fue hasta su actuación en Live Fight en 1985 que la canción se volvería popular."

podcast.body: This powerful title track from Bowie's 1977 album features artsy lyrics about two lovers finding optimism amid a world collapsing into death, including references to swimming with dolphins. Its meaning is layered, drawing inspiration from producer Tony Visconti's embrace with German singer Antonia Moss by the Berlin Wall, the Otto Mueller painting "Lovers Between Garden Walls," Alberto Denti di Pagano's 1956 short story "A Grave for a Dolphin," and a dream Bowie had about swimming with dolphins followed by a day with his girlfriend Claire Shenstone in East Berlin, watching soldiers. Bowie confirmed seeing Visconti and Moss, and Shenstone claimed their day directly inspired elements like dolphins, the wall, and gun shooting. "So which is true? All of them, apparently."

podcast.body: This title track from Bowie's 1977 album is highlighted as the best known of his Krautrock-influenced Berlin period. The single's B-side, "V-2 Schneider," was famously named after Kraftwerk's Florian Schneider, directly acknowledging the German influence. "I'm going to play you the title track, but you should know that the B side of this single was called V Schneider, named after craftwork's Florian Schneider."

podcast.body: This title track from his *Heroes* album was produced by Brian Eno during Bowie's time in Berlin and exemplifies his embrace of electronics-driven music. Bowie notably recorded three versions of the song: in English, French, and German. "Bowie with the title track of his hero's album. Actually one of three versions he did in English and French and German."

podcast.body: The second verse of this iconic song was inspired by Bowie witnessing his producer, Tony Visconti, and a backup singer sharing a quick kiss by the Berlin Wall from the control room window of Hansa Studio. Bowie had told Visconti to take a walk so he could think alone to finish the lyrics for the song. "From the control room window Bowie saw Visconti and his girlfriend steal a quick kiss by the Berlin wall. And that's where the second verse of this song came from."

podcast.body: The title track of its album, "Heroes" had several alleged inspirations including a young couple kissing by the Berlin Wall (possibly producer Tony Visconti and Antonia Maass), Otto Mueller's 1916 painting "Lovers Between Garden Walls," a book called "A Grave for Adolfin," or time spent with a woman named Claire Shenstone. Bowie recorded the song in English, German, and French, reflecting his time in Berlin. "The title track was allegedly inspired by something Bowie saw from the studio window one day. The young couple, meaning by the Berlin Wall for a kiss."
